title: Microservice Production Deployment Runbook
text: A production deployment of a microservice begins by merging to the main branch, which triggers the build pipeline. A production deployment requires one approving reviewer on the merge request. The pipeline builds an immutable container image, signs it, and pushes it to the internal registry. Rollout uses a canary strategy: five percent of traffic is shifted to the new revision for a ten-minute canary window while error rate and p99 latency are compared against the baseline. If the canary is healthy the rollout proceeds in twenty-five percent increments. Automated rollback is triggered when the error rate exceeds one percent for two consecutive minutes.

title: Service Onboarding Checklist for New Microservices
text: Before a new microservice may receive production traffic it must satisfy the platform onboarding checklist. The service must declare an owning team and an on-call rotation. It must expose a health endpoint at /healthz and a readiness endpoint at /readyz. It must emit structured JSON logs, OpenTelemetry traces, and the four golden-signal metrics. Resource requests and limits must be set explicitly; services without limits are rejected by the admission controller. A service-level objective must be registered with the reliability team. Finally, the service must pass a dependency scan and a container image vulnerability scan with no critical findings.

title: Infrastructure as Code Standards
text: All infrastructure is provisioned through version-controlled Terraform modules. Manual changes through the cloud console are prohibited and are reverted automatically by the drift detector within one hour. Each environment has its own state backend with state locking enabled. Module changes are validated by terraform plan in continuous integration and the plan output is attached to the merge request for review. Applying to production is gated behind a protected pipeline stage. Secrets are never stored in Terraform variables; they are referenced from the secrets manager at runtime.

title: Observability and Log Retention Runbook
text: Telemetry is stored in three tiers. Application logs are retained for 90 days in the hot tier where they are fully indexed and searchable. Traces are sampled at one percent in steady state and retained for 30 days. Metrics are downsampled after 14 days and kept for 13 months to support year-over-year capacity planning. Engineers can raise the trace sample rate to one hundred percent for a single service for up to one hour during an active incident. Log queries spanning more than seven days should use the archive search API because interactive search is rate limited.

title: API Performance Troubleshooting Guide
text: Begin API latency triage by confirming the symptom in the golden-signal dashboard and identifying whether p50 or only p99 latency has regressed. A p99-only regression usually indicates lock contention, garbage collection pauses, or a slow dependency affecting a subset of requests. Next, decompose latency by span using distributed traces to find the dominant contributor. Check the database layer for slow queries, missing indexes, and connection-pool saturation, which presents as rising wait time with flat query time. Inspect downstream call timeouts and retry budgets, since aggressive retries amplify load and convert a brownout into an outage. Confirm whether the regression correlates with a recent deployment, a configuration change, or a traffic-shape change.

title: Deep Request Diagnostics
text: When span-level traces are insufficient to explain a latency spike, enable verbose request tracing in production to diagnose latency spikes. Verbose tracing captures full request and response payloads, all header values, and per-middleware timing, which makes it possible to attribute latency to serialization, authentication, or payload size. Enable it for a single pod using the diagnostics flag, collect two to five minutes of samples, then disable it. Verbose tracing increases log volume by roughly forty times and adds measurable CPU overhead, so it must never be left enabled across an entire fleet.

title: API Gateway Rate Limiting and Timeout Configuration
text: The API gateway enforces a default request timeout of 30 seconds and a per-client rate limit of 1000 requests per minute. Services with stricter needs declare overrides in their service manifest. Client timeouts must always be shorter than the gateway timeout to avoid orphaned work. Retries use exponential backoff with full jitter and are capped at three attempts, and every retry must carry an idempotency key. Circuit breakers open after fifty percent failures over a twenty-request rolling window and half-open after thirty seconds. Load shedding activates at eighty-five percent CPU and returns HTTP 503 with a Retry-After header.

title: Database Performance and Connection Management
text: Each service instance opens a bounded connection pool; total connections across all replicas must stay under seventy percent of the database maximum to leave headroom for migrations and administrative sessions. Statement timeout defaults to 15 seconds for interactive queries and is raised explicitly for batch jobs. Queries exceeding 200 milliseconds are logged to the slow query log and reviewed weekly. Before adding an index, verify selectivity with an explain analyze plan, because low-selectivity indexes increase write amplification without improving reads. Schema migrations must be backward compatible for one release so that rollback does not require a data migration.

title: Microservice Architecture Guidelines
text: A microservice owns its data store exclusively; cross-service access to another service's database is prohibited and must be replaced by an explicit API or an event stream. Service boundaries follow business capabilities rather than technical layers. Synchronous call chains deeper than three services are flagged in architecture review because they multiply latency and failure probability. Prefer asynchronous events for workflows that tolerate eventual consistency. Every public interface is versioned, and breaking changes require a parallel version with a documented deprecation window of at least two quarters.

title: Secrets Management and Workload Identity
text: Workloads authenticate using short-lived identity tokens issued by the platform identity provider; long-lived static credentials are not issued for service-to-service calls. Secrets are stored in the central secrets manager and injected as memory-backed files rather than environment variables, because environment variables leak into crash dumps and process listings. Secret rotation is automated on a 90-day cycle and services must reload credentials without a restart. Any credential that appears in a log, a trace, or a ticket is treated as compromised and rotated immediately.

title: Continuous Integration Pipeline Reference
text: The continuous integration pipeline runs seven stages: lint, unit tests, build, image scan, integration tests, contract tests, and publish. Unit tests must complete within five minutes and maintain at least eighty percent line coverage on changed files. Contract tests validate both consumer and provider sides against the shared schema registry and block merges on incompatible changes. Flaky tests are quarantined automatically after three non-deterministic failures within a week and raise a ticket for the owning team. Build artifacts are content-addressed so identical inputs reuse cached results.

title: Kubernetes Workload Configuration Standards
text: Workloads declare CPU and memory requests that reflect observed p95 usage plus thirty percent headroom. Memory limits equal requests to avoid eviction surprises, while CPU is left burstable. Horizontal autoscaling targets seventy percent CPU utilization with a minimum of two replicas so that a single node failure cannot take a service offline. Pod disruption budgets permit at most one unavailable replica during voluntary disruptions. Anti-affinity rules spread replicas across availability zones. Liveness probes must be cheap and must not depend on downstream services, because a dependency outage would otherwise cascade into mass pod restarts.

title: Incident Response Runbook
text: Incidents are classified from SEV1, a full customer-facing outage, through SEV4, a minor degradation with no customer impact. SEV1 and SEV2 incidents page the on-call engineer immediately and open a dedicated channel with an assigned incident commander. The first priority is mitigation, not diagnosis: roll back, shift traffic, or disable the offending feature flag before investigating root cause. Every SEV1 and SEV2 requires a blameless postmortem within five business days with corrective actions tracked as tickets. Customer communication for SEV1 is owned by the support lead, not the engineer on call.

title: Event Streaming and Message Delivery
text: The event bus guarantees at-least-once delivery, so every consumer must be idempotent and deduplicate on the event identifier. Events are immutable facts named in the past tense and carry a schema version. Ordering is guaranteed only within a partition key, so workflows that require ordering must choose a partition key that matches their aggregate. Consumers that fall more than one hundred thousand messages behind raise a lag alert. Poison messages are routed to a dead-letter topic after five failed attempts and must be triaged within one business day.

title: Load Testing and Capacity Planning
text: Load tests run against a production-shaped staging environment with representative data volume, because synthetic empty datasets hide index and cache behaviour. A test ramps to the target rate over five minutes, holds for thirty minutes, and records p50, p95, and p99 latency along with error rate and saturation signals. The reported capacity figure is the highest sustained rate at which p99 latency stays within the service-level objective, not the rate at which the service stops responding. Capacity headroom of forty percent above peak observed traffic is required before a seasonal event.

title: Caching Strategy Guide
text: Read-through caching is the default pattern for read-heavy endpoints, with a short time to live and jittered expiry to avoid synchronized stampedes. Write-through caching is reserved for data that must never serve a stale read. Cache keys include the schema version so a deployment that changes a payload shape does not read incompatible entries. A cache hit ratio below eighty percent on a hot endpoint usually indicates a key cardinality problem rather than an undersized cache. Never cache authorization decisions longer than the token lifetime.

title: Data Pipeline Implementation Patterns
text: A new data processing workflow is implemented as a directed acyclic graph of idempotent tasks so that any task can be retried without duplicating effects. Each task declares its inputs and outputs as datasets, which lets the scheduler derive dependencies and backfill ranges automatically. Landing data is written once in raw form and never mutated; transformations produce new versioned datasets. Data quality checks on row count, null rate, and referential integrity run as blocking gates before a dataset is published. Personal data fields must be tagged in the dataset schema so downstream masking can be applied automatically.
